vignette:
Koa, a man of forty-five with a quiet strength that once defined him, carried the weight of a life irrevocably altered. A chef by trade, his hands, once deft and confident, now often felt foreign to him, a source of unease. The traumatic event, a brutal rape that had occurred late one night in the deserted alleyway behind his own restaurant, had stripped him of a fundamental sense of self. He remembered the metallic tang of fear in his mouth, the cold brick against his back, and the searing violation that followed.

In the aftermath, Koa found he could talk about what happened very easily, almost too easily. He would recount the details to anyone who asked, a flat, dispassionate recitation of facts, as if narrating someone else's story. Yet, beneath this surface fluency, a profound disorganization churned. When pressed for a specific timeline or to elaborate on certain moments, he would falter, the sequence of events jumbling and blurring in his mind. He found himself unable to put the memories of the event in the right order, often jumping from one fragmented image to another without logical progression. Worse still, just as a clearer, more complete recollection seemed within reach, a sudden mental fog would descend. He would feel an invisible hand pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, leaving him with an unsettling blend of clarity and frustrating blanks.

The kitchen, once his sanctuary, became a crucible for his torment. The smell of raw meat, the slickness of oil on his hands, the sudden clang of a dropped pot – each could conjure a fleeting, disorienting fragment of that night. What frightened him most was the pervasive feeling that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. His once intuitive understanding of flavors seemed dulled, his precision in plating faltered, and the creative spark that had fuelled his successful career had guttered to an ember. He would stand before a simmering pot, his mind blank, certain that he had forgotten how to cook, how to lead his team, how to be the chef he once was.

A profound sense of feeling dirty or contaminated because of what happened seeped into every corner of Koa’s existence. He washed his hands obsessively, scrubbing until his skin was raw, yet the feeling lingered, an internal stain that no amount of soap could remove. He found himself increasingly repulsed by certain textures and ingredients, particularly anything that felt slippery or viscous, making the preparation of many dishes a daily ordeal. He started to doubt the purity of the food he prepared, a subtle, insidious fear that he might somehow transfer his own perceived defilement onto it, making him hesitant to serve his creations to his customers. This fear, coupled with his growing self-doubt, meant he gradually withdrew from the hands-on aspects of his kitchen, delegating more and more, losing the direct connection to his craft that had once been his joy.

Over months, this combination of memory fragmentation, self-doubt, and pervasive contamination beliefs began to erode his life. His restaurant, once a vibrant hub, suffered from his diminished presence and flagging passion. Regulars noticed his distant demeanor, and his once-loyal staff grew confused by his erratic behavior and sudden outbursts of frustration when he couldn't recall a recipe detail or felt overwhelmed by a simple task. His divorce, which had occurred some years prior, meant he had no immediate partner to lean on, and his increasing isolation only amplified his inner conviction: his life has been destroyed by the trauma. He saw no path forward, no way to reclaim the man he was, or to rebuild the career he had painstakingly built. The cumulative weight of these feelings, the realization that he was merely existing, a shadow in his own kitchen, finally prompted Koa to seek help, hoping against hope that perhaps, despite everything, some part of him could still be salvaged.
